goals: Fit and interpret a regression with several features
why: Real outcomes have many drivers. Multiple regression separates their effects, for example how much of a price premium comes from location versus size.
explain: The model becomes **ŷ = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + …**. Each coefficient is the expected change in y for a one-unit change in that feature **with all other features held fixed**.
That "holding fixed" is the superpower: simple regression of price on bedrooms mixes up bedrooms and size; multiple regression separates them.

**Multicollinearity**: when features are highly correlated (area and number of rooms), coefficients become unstable and can even flip sign. Check the **VIF** (variance inflation factor); above 5–10 is a warning.
Use **adjusted R²** or cross-validation to compare models. Plain R² always rises when you add a feature, even a useless one.

formula.tex: \hat y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + \dots + b_p x_p, \qquad \hat b = (X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}y
formula.plain: A starting value plus a weighted sum of the features; the coefficients are found by least squares (matrix form on the right).

example.title: Pricing a flat with three features
steps: Least squares on eight flats gives: price = 5.5 + 3.97 × area(100 sq ft) − 0.51 × age(years) + 7.72 × near_metro(0/1)
Flat: 1,000 sq ft, 8 years old, near the metro
Reading: being near the metro is worth about ₹7.7L at the same size and age; each year of age takes off about ₹51,000
example.result: About ₹48.8 lakh. Each coefficient answers a separate business question, provided the features are not strongly collinear.

mistakes: Comparing raw coefficient sizes across features with different units (standardise first).
Adding features until R² looks great (overfitting).
takeaways: Compare models with adjusted R² or CV
interview: What is multicollinearity and how do you detect it?
Why does R² always increase when you add features?

practice.code:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
flats = pd.DataFrame({'area': [6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15], 'age': [4, 15, 6, 3, 18, 9, 12, 7],
                      'near_metro': [0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1],
                      'price': [27.5, 37.1, 38.3, 51.0, 40.4, 56.7, 54.4, 69.6]})
X, y = flats[['area', 'age', 'near_metro']], flats['price']
m = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
print(round(m.intercept_, 2), pd.Series(m.coef_, index=X.columns).round(2).to_dict())
print(m.predict(pd.DataFrame({'area': [10], 'age': [8], 'near_metro': [1]})).round(1))   # [48.8]

options: Each extra year lowers the price by about ₹0.51L, holding other features fixed
check.why: Partial effect, other variables held constant.

check.q: VIF of 15 for a feature suggests…
check.why: VIF above 10 signals that the feature is largely explained by the others.
